## Report: Does Denosumab (Prolia) Reduce Vertebral Fracture Risk?

Your sister is correct — the evidence strongly supports that denosumab reduces vertebral fracture risk in osteoporosis, though there's an important caveat about treatment continuity.

**Primary evidence:** The pivotal FREEDOM trial (Cummings et al., NEJM 2009), a large international randomized, placebo-controlled study in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis, found that denosumab given subcutaneously every 6 months for 36 months reduced the risk of new vertebral fractures by 68%, hip fractures by 40%, and nonvertebral fractures by 20% compared to placebo (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/nejmoa0809493). This is a high-quality, well-powered RCT and remains the cornerstone of denosumab's fracture-prevention evidence.

**Long-term data:** The FREEDOM Extension study followed women for up to 10 years and showed sustained bone mineral density gains and persistently low vertebral fracture rates compared to a modeled "virtual placebo" cohort, reinforcing durability of benefit with continued treatment (https://www.thelancet.com/journals/landia/article/PIIS2213-8587(17)30138-9/fulltext).

**Independent confirmation:** A 2023 systematic review and network meta-analysis comparing denosumab to bisphosphonates, SERMs, and placebo confirmed denosumab's efficacy in reducing fractures, including vertebral fractures, across the broader evidence base (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00223-023-01078-z).

**Important caveat:** Post hoc analysis of FREEDOM and its extension revealed that stopping denosumab causes a "rebound" effect — rapid bone turnover and bone loss that can lead to multiple vertebral fractures, sometimes exceeding pre-treatment risk (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5915244/).

**Conclusion:** Yes — denosumab clearly reduces vertebral fracture risk while being used, per rigorous RCT evidence. However, discontinuation without transitioning to another antiresorptive can rebound that risk, so ongoing management matters.
